case.presentation: Patient is a 44-year old man who had a positive quantiferon as part of a routine medical examination given he is from an endemic country. He has no symptoms and no known TB exposures. His chest-xray was negative for infection during his clinic visit today. He would like to delay TB treatment if not absolutely necessary for at least a few months. Does this patient need immediate TB treatment and if so, with what regimen?
case.recommendations: The patient likely has latent TB. From a public health perspective, this should be non-urgently treated due to risk for reactivation TB. This can be done non-urgently given patient has no clear risk factors for reactivation. The patient should be counseled that latent TB is not infectious, though close contacts or family with similar exposure history may also benefit from testing. An HIV test should be ordered; if the HIV test is positive, that would warrant more urgent treatment. Baseline liver function tests and renal function tests should be ordered if proceeding with treatment. Recommended treatment is rifampin 600 mg daily x 4 months given it is well-tolerated. Alternative regimens include isoniazid 300 mg PO daily for 9 months or rifapentine 900 mg PO weekly with isoniazid 900 mg PO weekly for 12 weeks; if an INH-containing regimen is chosen, add pyridoxine 25 mg daily and counsel avoidance of alcohol. The patient can also be seen non-urgently in ID clinic and treatment can be discussed at that time as well.
